concepts.title: Data Bias and Shift
concepts.one_liner: Failures in machine learning often stem from the discrepancy between the theoretical assumption of identically distributed data and the reality of data shift.
concepts.content: The goal of learning is to acquire rules from past data that work well on future data. In the theory of machine learning, it is almost always assumed that the future is *identically distributed* as the past. In reality, it is almost always the case that this is not true. Many of the failures of machine learning in industry and in society are due to this discrepancy between theory and practice. It is critical to understand what happens when a learned system is deployed on data that is unlike what it was trained on.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding data bias and shift is essential for building robust models that can handle real-world scenarios where future data inevitably differs from training data.
concepts.recap_md: - Machine learning theory often assumes training and test data are identically distributed.

concepts.title: Dataset Bias
concepts.one_liner: Dataset bias occurs because every dataset offers a different and biased sample of the visual world based on its collection strategy.
concepts.content: Bias is present in all datasets. Even datasets that try to cover the same aspect of the world collect data with different styles and strategies that reflect on the statistics of the dataset. In the case of image datasets for computer vision, the goal is to represent the visual world with all its complexity and diversity. Despite that there is a single visual world, different computer vision datasets offer a different, and biased, sample of that world.
concepts.motivation_md: Recognizing dataset bias is the first step in understanding why models trained on one dataset may fail to generalize to others, even if they target the same domain.
concepts.recap_md: - All datasets contain inherent biases based on their collection strategies.

concepts.title: Annotation Bias
concepts.one_liner: Annotation bias arises from the choices annotators make regarding which images to label and which language to use.
concepts.content: When annotating images, image annotators will choose which images to annotate and which labels to use. This will also correlate with viewpoint preferences and other photographer biases, as those images might be easier to annotate and segment, risking a compounding effect with photographer bias. Annotations require making language choices that are an important source of bias, especially social bias.
concepts.motivation_md: Annotation bias highlights how human subjectivity in the labeling process introduces systematic errors and social biases into machine learning models.
concepts.recap_md: - Annotator choices regarding images and labels introduce systematic bias.

concepts.title: Social Bias
concepts.one_liner: Social bias refers to the different and often stereotypical ways groups of people are reflected in data and labels.
concepts.content: Social bias refers to biases associated with how groups of people might be reflected differently in the data. This type of bias can affect both the images and the associated labels. Social biases can originate from the data collection protocol or from existing social biases; for example, images may be captured in certain world regions or contain stereotypes. Labels can also reflect social assumptions, such as a dataset that associates doctors with males and nurses with females. These biases can have a negative social impact once models are deployed, making it important to incorporate techniques to mitigate their effects.
concepts.motivation_md: Addressing social bias is crucial for ensuring that AI systems are fair, ethical, and do not reinforce harmful stereotypes when deployed in society.
concepts.recap_md: - Social bias stems from data collection protocols and existing societal stereotypes.

motivation.text: These types of biases, besides impacting the overall model performance, can have a negative social impact once they are deployed. It is important to be aware of those biases, and incorporate techniques to mitigate their effects.

concepts.title: Testing and Benchmark Bias
concepts.one_liner: Biases in the test set can negatively impact system behavior because researchers use them to decide which algorithms or data collections are most effective.
concepts.content: Biases in the test set can have an even more negative impact on final system behavior than training bias. The test set is what researchers and engineers use to decide which algorithm is best, or what data collection is more effective for training. However, there might be little correlation between the performance measured on the test set and the final performance of the system during deployment. In particular, if we compare two training datasets, one biased and another less biased, by evaluating the performance of a system trained on them using a biased test dataset, we could reach the conclusion that the biased dataset is better.
concepts.motivation_md: Evaluation metrics are only as reliable as the data they are measured on. If a test set is biased, it can mislead developers into choosing models that perform well on the benchmark but fail in real-world deployment.
concepts.recap_md: - Biased test sets can lead to incorrect conclusions about which training data or algorithms are superior.

concepts.title: Adversarial attacks
concepts.one_liner: Adversarial attacks involve adding imperceptible noise to data to force a neural network to produce a specific, incorrect output.
concepts.content: Adversarial attacks occur when an attacker adds imperceptible noise to an image that fools neural net classifiers despite looking completely innocuous to a human. The noise pattern can be selected to force the network to produce any output the attacker desires. The adversary can do this by optimizing the noise pattern to cause the network to make a particular output, while restricting the noise to be very subtle, typically within a small $r$-radius ball around the original image. For example, to cause an image classifier $f$ to think the cat in (see figure: An adversarial attack that adds subtle changes to the cat photo to make a neural net classify it instead as an ostrich. The noise image color values are scaled 20x for visualization.) is an ostrich, the attacker could find the noise pattern via the following optimization: $$\begin{aligned} \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_{\mathbf{\epsilon}} H(\mathbf{y}_{\texttt{ostrich}}, f(\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{\epsilon})), \quad\quad \text{subject to} \quad\quad \left\lVert\mathbf{\epsilon}\right\rVert < r \end{aligned}$$ where $H$ is the cross-entropy loss and $\mathbf{y}_{\texttt{ostrich}}$ is a one-hot code for the ostrich class.
concepts.motivation_md: Neural networks are often sensitive to small, targeted perturbations that humans cannot see. Understanding these attacks is crucial for building secure systems that cannot be easily manipulated by malicious actors.
concepts.recap_md: - Adversarial attacks use optimized, subtle noise to manipulate model outputs.

key_passage.text: These are called adversarial attacks because we suppose the attacker, who adds the noise, is an adversary that wants to fool or manipulate your system. The adversary can do this by simply optimizing the noise pattern to cause the network to make a particular output, while restricting the noise to be very subtle (within an small r-radius ball around the original image).

motivation.text: This was famously demonstrated by Szegedy et al., who showed that one can add imperceptible noise to an image that fools neural net classifiers despite looking completely innocuous to a human. In fact, the noise pattern can be selected to force the network to produce any output the attacker desires.

concepts.title: Adversarial robustness
concepts.one_liner: Adversarial robustness refers to a system's ability to minimize worst-case error rather than just the average error over training data.
concepts.content: Adversarial analysis is worst-case analysis. Typically, systems are trained to minimize empirical risk, defined as the mean error over the training data. Because the focus is only on the mean, the worst case might be arbitrarily bad. Alternative approaches try to minimize worst-case error, which can result in systems that are more adversarially robust.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard training focuses on average performance, which leaves models vulnerable to specific, targeted failures. Robustness aims to guarantee a certain level of performance even under the most difficult or manipulated conditions.
concepts.recap_md: - Adversarial robustness focuses on minimizing the worst-case error rather than the mean empirical risk.

concepts.title: Adversarial training
concepts.one_liner: Adversarial training is a technique that increases model robustness by training on worst-case transformations rather than random ones.
concepts.content: Adversarial training can be used to increase the robustness of models to adversarial attacks. While standard data augmentation applies random transformations to the data to do well in expectation, adversarial training considers augmenting with worst-case transformations that incur the highest loss possible for a given training example: $$\begin{aligned} \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_f \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}} [\max_{\theta \in \Theta}[\mathcal{L}(f(T(\mathbf{x};\theta)),\mathbf{y})]] \end{aligned}$$ This increases the robustness of the learned function $f$ to perturbations that may occur at test time. In the context of adversarial robustness, one form of this is to set $T$ to be an epsilon-ball attack, where $T(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}+\mathbf{\epsilon}$: $$\begin{aligned} \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_f \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}} [\max_{\mathbf{\epsilon} \, s.t. \left\lVert\mathbf{\epsilon}\right\rVert < r}[\mathcal{L}(f(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{\epsilon}),\mathbf{y})]] \end{aligned}$$ This can increase robustness against the kinds of epsilon-ball attacks seen in adversarial analysis.
concepts.motivation_md: To defend against adversarial attacks, models must be exposed to them during training. By solving a minimax problem, the model learns to handle the most difficult perturbations it might encounter.
concepts.recap_md: - Adversarial training replaces random data augmentation with worst-case perturbations.

key_passage.text: Instead of doing random transformations, we could instead consider augmenting with worst case transformations, applying those transformations that incur the highest loss possible for a given training example.

motivation.text: One of its effects is that it can increase the robustness of the learned function f to perturbations that may occur at test time (like those we saw in the previous chapter).

concepts.title: Model adaptation
concepts.one_liner: Model adaptation, also known as transfer learning, is a strategy for dealing with dataset bias and shift by adjusting a model to new domains.
concepts.content: There are two general ways of dealing with dataset bias and shift. The first is called domain randomization, or data augmentation. The second is called transfer learning, or model adaptation.
concepts.motivation_md: When a model is trained on one distribution but must perform on another, model adaptation provides a way to bridge the gap without starting training from scratch.
concepts.recap_md: - Model adaptation is a primary strategy for addressing dataset shift and bias.

key_passage.text: The second is called transfer learning, or model adaptation.

concepts.title: Data augmentation
concepts.one_liner: Data augmentation increases the size and diversity of a dataset by adding synthetic pairs created through random transformations of the original data.
concepts.content: Data augmentation is a method for dealing with dataset bias and shift by adding random transformations of each datapoint. For example, common augmentations can be applied to an image, as shown in (see figure: A few common types of data augmentation.). By mapping from a smaller dataset to a larger one, it simulates the effect of adding more real data. For each $\{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}, \mathbf{y}^{(i)}\}$ pair in the original dataset, you add $M$ new synthetic pairs $\{T(\mathbf{x}^{(i)};\theta^{(j)}), \mathbf{y}^{(i)}\}_{j=1}^M$, where $T$ is a transformation function with stochastic parameters $\theta \sim p_{\theta}$. For instance, if $T$ is a `crop` function, $\theta$ would be the coordinates specifying where to apply the crop.
concepts.motivation_md: Machine learning models require large amounts of data to generalize well. Data augmentation allows practitioners to artificially expand their datasets, improving model performance and robustness to variations.
concepts.recap_md: - Data augmentation creates synthetic training examples using stochastic transformations like cropping or rotating.

key_passage.text: augments a dataset by adding random transformations of each datapoint. When you do this for every image in a dataset, you are essentially mapping from a smaller dataset to a larger dataset. The way data augmentation works is that for each pair in your original dataset, you add M new synthetic pairs, where T is a data transformation function with stochastic parameters.

motivation.text: We know that more data is usually better, so this is a way to simulate the effect of adding more real data to your dataset. Data augmentation is like a philosopher's stone of machine learning: it converts lead (small data) into gold (big data).

concepts.title: Domain randomization
concepts.one_liner: Domain randomization is a technique used with simulators to randomize parameters, creating a broader set of experiences for a learner.
concepts.content: Domain randomization is an idea analogous to data augmentation used when data is generated by a simulator rather than a static dataset. Instead of adding random transformations to points in a dataset, we randomize the parameters of the simulator so that each interaction with the simulation will look slightly different. For example, lighting conditions may be randomized. This converts a narrow set of experiences, such as a simulation with one kind of lighting condition, to a much broader set of experiences to learn from.
concepts.motivation_md: Simulators often fail to capture the complexity of the real world. By randomizing simulation parameters, models can learn to be invariant to factors like lighting or texture, easing the transfer to reality.
concepts.recap_md: - Domain randomization applies the principles of data augmentation to simulated environments.

key_passage.text: Here, rather than adding random transformations to points in a dataset, we instead randomize the parameters of the simulator, so that each interaction with the simulation will look slightly different, for example, the lighting conditions may be randomized.

concepts.title: Transfer learning
concepts.one_liner: Transfer learning uses prior knowledge from previously solved problems to accelerate learning on new, related tasks.
concepts.content: Transfer learning, also known as model adaptation, is a general way of dealing with dataset bias and shift. It provides the means to use priors to accelerate learning and deals with how to use prior knowledge to solve new learning problems quickly.
concepts.motivation_md: Training models from scratch is computationally expensive and requires massive datasets. Transfer learning allows us to leverage existing models to solve new problems with less data and time.
concepts.recap_md: - Transfer learning utilizes knowledge from one domain to improve learning in another.

key_passage.text: Transfer learning deals with how to use prior knowledge to solve new learning problems quickly.
